title: AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
key_facts: Brad Smith, president of Microsoft, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast that milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI.

He called for global safety rules, including a legal duty to tell a 'victim' when their system is breached by a rogue AI agent, and rules on when outside evaluators must sign off an AI product before release.

He said companies need 'emergency brakes', often called kill switches, to pause or slow AI that gets out of control, and a legal duty to write 'incident reports'; he also suggested independent government evaluators should vet new AI.
The BBC says his views put him at odds with President Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals.
Smith said the UK is best placed to drive global rules because of its AI Security Institute, and that Washington looks at London differently from Brussels.

At the end of last month Trump hosted the leaders of OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google, who signed a 'morally binding' document to work with independent auditors; Smith called it 'a good step, a necessary step' but said 'I don't think it's sufficient any longer'.
Smith said the problem with self-regulation is that 'the good companies will do what you want' and the worry is 'the companies that are not as responsible'.
quote_evidence: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."
He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way.
"It's a good step, it's a necessary step... But I don't think it's sufficient any longer."
why_it_matters_hint: A head of one of the biggest AI companies asks for binding safety rules, against the White House line of self-regulation.
event_date: Interview date not stated; BBC published it 11 Oct 2026 (late UTC)
